content: 1. Amphotericin B cholesteryl sulfate should be administered intravenously at a dose of 3 mg/kg every 24 hours. Induction therapy should last for at least 2 weeks or until clinical improvement is observed. 2. Maintenance therapy options include: Preferred regimen: Itraconazole 200 mg orally three times daily for 3 days, followed by 200 mg orally twice daily for 12 months. Alternative regimens: 1. Voriconazole 400 mg orally twice daily for 1 day, then 200 mg orally twice daily. 2. Posaconazole 400 mg orally twice daily. 3. Fluconazole 800 mg orally once daily. 3. For meningitis: Induction therapy: Liposomal amphotericin B at 5 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks. Maintenance therapy: Itraconazole 200 mg orally twice to three times daily for at least 1 year. Treatment should continue until cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities resolve. 4. Long-term suppression therapy: Preferred regimen: Itraconazole 200 mg orally once daily. Alternative regimen: Fluconazole 400 mg orally once daily. Note: 5. For coccidioidomycosis: Prevention: Patients with a new positive IgM or IgG serologic test who live in endemic areas and have a CD4 count <250 cells/µL should receive fluconazole 400 mg orally once daily. 6. Treatment of clinically mild infections (e.g., focal pneumonia): Preferred regimen: Fluconazole 400 mg orally once daily or itraconazole 200 mg orally twice daily. Alternative regimens: Posaconazole 200 mg orally twice daily or voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily. 7. For severe, non-meningeal infections (e.g., diffuse pulmonary infection or severe disseminated disease): Preferred regimen: Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1.0 mg/kg intravenously daily or lipid formulation amphotericin B 4–6 mg/kg intravenously daily. Alternative regimen: Fluconazole or itraconazole (preferred for bone disease) 400 mg daily after amphotericin B therapy, continuing triazole therapy once amphotericin B is stopped. 8. For meningeal infections: Preferred regimen: Fluconazole 400–800 mg intravenously or orally once daily. Alternative regimens: Itraconazole 200 mg orally three times daily for 3 days, then 200 mg orally twice daily; posaconazole 200 mg orally twice daily; or voriconazole 200–400 mg orally twice daily. 9. Chronic suppressive therapy: Preferred regimen: Fluconazole 400 mg orally once daily or itraconazole 200 mg orally twice daily. Alternative regimens: Posaconazole 200 mg orally twice daily or voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily. Note: Therapy should be continued indefinitely in patients with diffuse pulmonary or disseminated diseases due to a relapse rate of 25–33% in HIV-negative patients. Lifelong therapy is recommended for meningitis, as relapse occurs in 80% of HIV-infected patients after discontinuation of triazole therapy. 10. For herpes simplex virus (HSV) disease: Orolabial lesions (5–10 days): Valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily. Famciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily. Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily. Initial or recurrent genital HSV (5–14 days): Valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily. Famciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily. Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily. Severe mucocutaneous HSV: Initial therapy: Acyclovir 5 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours. Switch to oral therapy once lesions regress and continue until complete healing. Chronic suppressive therapy: Valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily. Famciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily. Acyclovir 400 mg orally twice daily. For acyclovir-resistant HSV: Preferred therapy: Foscarnet 80–120 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8–12 hours. Alternative regimens: Cidofovir intravenously or topical trifluridine or imiquimod for 21–28 days. Note: Therapy should continue indefinitely regardless of CD4 count. 11. For varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection: Prevention: Patients with CD4 counts ≥200 cells/µL who are unvaccinated, have no history of varicella or herpes zoster, or are seronegative for VZV should receive primary varicella vaccination (2 doses of 0.5 mL subcutaneously, 3 months apart). Household contacts of susceptible HIV-infected individuals should also be vaccinated. Alternatively, acyclovir 800 mg orally daily for 5–7 days or valacyclovir 1 g orally three times daily for 5–7 days may be used. Note: Routine VZV serologic testing in HIV-infected adults and adolescents is not recommended. If vaccination results in disease due to the vaccine virus, treatment with acyclovir is recommended. 12. Treatment of primary varicella infection (chickenpox): Uncomplicated cases (5–7 days): Valacyclovir 1 g orally three times daily. Famciclovir 500 mg orally three times daily. Severe or complicated cases: Preferred regimen: Acyclovir 10–15 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours for 7–10 days. Alternative regimen: Acyclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 5–7 days. 13. Treatment of herpes zoster (shingles): Acute localized dermatomal: Valacyclovir 1 g orally three times daily for 7–10 days (longer duration if lesions resolve slowly). Famciclovir 500 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days (longer duration if lesions resolve slowly). Extensive cutaneous lesions or visceral involvement: Preferred regimen: Acyclovir 10–15 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours until clinical improvement, then switch to oral therapy (valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir) to complete a 10–14 day course. Alternative regimen: Acyclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 7–10 days (longer duration if lesions resolve slowly). 14. For progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN): Preferred regimen: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg with or without foscarnet 90 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, combined with ganciclovir 2 mg/0.05 mL with or without foscarnet 1.2 mg/0.05 mL intravitreal injection biweekly. 15. For acute retinal necrosis (ARN): Preferred regimen: Acyclovir 10–15 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours, combined with ganciclovir 2 mg/0.05 mL intravitreal injection (1–2 doses biweekly for 10–14 days).
